paper_title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Memory serves as the foundation for experiential and continual intelligence (Hassabis et al., 2017; Sumers et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025). As large language models (LLMs) transition from single-turn processing toward continual interactions and long-horizon agent tasks, maintaining reusable memory states is essential to eliminate redundant context recomputation and ensure low-latency response generation (Xi et al., 2025; Chhikara et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026). However, existing architectures face fundamental trade-off between retention fidelity and inference scalability. Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) with global attention retain layer-wise, token-level key-value (KV) caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, recurrent and linear models (e.g., Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023), RWKV (Peng et al., 2023), and GDN (Yang et al., 2025)) compress history into fixed-size states to enable constant-memory, linear-time inference; yet their bounded state capacity can induce information decay, hindering the preservation of fine-grained details over long horizons (Jelassi et al., 2024). Extensive efforts have sought to reconcile this trade-off, broadly falling into three categories: (1) Architectural and attention optimizations: hybrid models (e.g., Kimi K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026) and MiMo-V2.6 (Qiao et al., 2026)) interleave attention and linear layers, cross-layer sharing approaches (Sun et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2026a) reuse intermediate KV caches, and sparse attention mechanisms (e.g., DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Xu et al., 2026a) and Qwen3.8-Next (Qiu et al., 2026)) restrict attention to top-k relevant tokens. However, during continual inference, they still need to maintain or access global caches that grow linearly with context length. (2) Native memory models: parametric memory designs (e.g., Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025), M+ (Wang et al., 2025a), and Metis (Zhang et al., 2026)) compress historical context into compact memory representations via specialized training or post-training adaptation. Yet, they often suffer from performance degradation, layer-wise retrieval overhead, or catastrophic forgetting. (3) External memory systems: agentic memory frameworks (e.g., Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026b), and PersonaVLM (Nie et al., 2026b)) organize historical context into explicit databases that can be managed, updated, and queried. Nevertheless, constructing and maintaining these discrete stores is costly (Nie et al., 2026c) and difficult to optimize end-to-end (Wang et al., 2025b). Despite these efforts, central question remains open: How can we build foundational memory architecture (or adapt an existing one) to simultaneously achieve accurate recall, linear-time inference, and bounded GPU memory cache overhead for continual inference? In this paper, we propose MemOnce, an expressive yet scalable architecture that learns reusable memory states for language models. The core idea of MemOnce is to maintain single compact global cache and retrieve relevant memory only once during continual inference to decode layer-wise KV caches, thereby enabling memory on-demand loading and decoding. Specifically, we first develop memory encoder-decoder that caches small subset (e.g., 1/8) of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations, dynamically decoding them via lightweight MLPs into KV caches for attention layers. This design achieves cache recurrence and an Lr compression across both depth and time dimensions. Second, we introduce memory sparse attention, which adaptively selects the top-K task-relevant states for each input and shares the sparse routing indices across all attention layers and decoding steps. By coupling these two designs, MemOnce achieves strong expressiveness, linear-time complexity, and constant active memory state (see Figure 1). We conduct extensive experiments across diverse tasks, model sizes, and context scales to demonstrate the superiority of MemOnce. Specifically, we highlight three key results: (1) MemOnce as foundation architecture: We train MemOnce and other foundation architectures from scratch across model sizes ranging from 150M to 1B parameters. MemOnce consistently achieves lower or comparable perplexity on validation data and performs well on downstream benchmarks compared to evaluated baselines (e.g., Transformer, GDN, and YOCO (Vaswani et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024b)). (2) MemOnce as native memory model: We adapt Qwen3.5 via post-training and evaluate it on five memory benchmarks spanning 4K to 1M tokens. As shown in Figure 1, MemOnce is the first native memory model to surpass the full-context baseline (+5.77% at the 4B scale) (Qwen Team, 2026), and outperforms prior memory methods (by +18.68% over M+ (Wang et al., 2025a) and +32.27% over Metis (Zhang et al., 2026)). At 1M context, it reduces memory state cache by 1313 and prefill latency by 6.9, and improves throughput by 3.5. Moreover, MemOnce avoids catastrophic forgetting on general benchmarks by keeping its parameters frozen during inference and inherently ignoring irrelevant decoded caches. (3) MemOnce as representation model: We show that 2 MemOnces learned memory representations transfer naturally to downstream retrieval and reranking tasks, outperforming specialized models without task-specific fine-tuning. These findings underscore the potential of MemOnce as next-generation general-purpose architecture. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We propose MemOnce, foundation architecture that achieves strong expressiveness, linear-time complexity, and constant active memory for continual inference. We couple two designs, memory encoder-decoder and memory sparse attention, to cache and retrieve memory representations only once for on-demand memory loading and KV cache decoding. We establish through comprehensive experiments that MemOnce advances the performancecomplexity Pareto frontier, marking the first native memory model to surpass the full-context baseline and generalizing zero-shot to downstream representation tasks.

Advantage Analysis. Compared with existing foundation architectures and native memory models,
MemOnce offers three key advantages: (1) Strong Performance: By maintaining an expandable memory bank
Gt and retrieving final-layer representations back into multi-layer KV caches, MemOnce overcomes fixed-
capacity bottlenecks and achieves accurate recall in long-context scenarios. (2) Bounded Active Memory State:
MemOnce reduces the persistent cache footprint by a factor of Lr and achieves constant active memory state
during continual inference. (3) High Inference Efficiency: As illustrated in Figure 1 (right), MemOnce operates
with linear-time complexity and achieves superior inference efficiency over existing memory architectures.

MemOnce supports end-to-end optimization under the standard next-token prediction paradigm for both pretraining and post-training adaptation. During pretraining, the backbone and memory encoder-decoder are jointly optimized, where historical segments are encoded in parallel into Gt and gradients flow directly through the active memory state Mt and the decoded KV caches. sections.title:
4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluation and Benchmarks. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate MemOnce across diverse
tasks, model scales, and context lengths. Our evaluation is organized into four primary tracks: (1) Foundational
Capability: We evaluate language modeling performance using perplexity (PPL) on WikiText (Merity et al.,
2017) and LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016). We further report zero-shot accuracy across eight downstream
tasks using the LM-Evaluation-Harness (Gao et al., 2021) to assess general knowledge and reasoning capabilities.
(2) Long-Context Memory Capability: We evaluate continual and long-horizon memory recall across context
lengths spanning 4K to 1M tokens on standard memory benchmarks, including MemBench (Tan et al., 2025),
LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025), and PersonaMem (Jiang et al., 2025).
(3) General Capability Retention: To measure general capability retention under active memory load and
verify robustness against catastrophic forgetting, we evaluate models on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021),
GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and GPQA (Rein et al., 2024). (4) Representation Tasks: Finally, we assess the
zero-shot generalizability of MemOnce’s learned memory representations on downstream text retrieval and
reranking benchmarks (Nie et al., 2026a).

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: (1) Foundational Capability. Joint recurrence and compression of context caches across depth and time enable MemOnce to cut the persistent cache footprint by Lr while delivering strong foundational performance. We report the results of pretraining different foundation architectures from scratch on FineWeb-Edu. As shown in Figure 3, MemOnce attains lower final validation perplexity than GDN, SWA, and YOCO, matches or surpasses the Transformer even at = 8, and achieves the best scaling performance from 0.15B to 1.0B parameters. In downstream evaluations  (Table 2)  , MemOncer=1 and MemOncer=8 attain the highest and second-highest average zero-shot accuracies across all evaluated architectures, while respectively achieving the lowest language modeling perplexities on WikiText-103 and LAMBADA. Notably, compressing the temporal dimension by 8 (MemOncer=8 vs. MemOncer=1) incurs virtually no performance loss, demonstrating that the model can effectively condense segment-level context into the trailing tokens while preserving essential long-range information. Crucially, whereas linear models (DeltaNet and GDN) degrade in language modeling perplexity due to fixed-state capacity bottlenecks and prior cache-sharing methods (YOCO and LastKV) lag behind in reasoning accuracy due to direct cross-layer reuse without learned decoding, MemOnce excels across both dimensions, validating its expressiveness as foundation architecture. (2) Long-Context Memory Capability. MemOnce is the first native memory model to surpass full-context baselines across model and context scales without suffering from catastrophic forgetting. Table 3 reports evaluation results across five long-context memory benchmarks spanning 4K to 1M tokens. Across both 2B and 4B scales, MemOnce surpasses its full-context Qwen3.5 counterparts with average scores of 51.17% (+1.84%) and 60.07% (+5.77%), respectively, as query-conditioned sparse retrieval filters out irrelevant historical context and mitigates the attention dilution inherent to ultra-long sequences. The memory representations learned by MemOnce transfer naturally to downstream retrieval and context reranking tasks, outperforming specialized embedding and reranking models. sections.title: 5.1 Why Existing Memory Architectures Fail to Scale
sections.content: Existing memory architectures (Wang et al., 2025a; Lei et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026) struggle to scale effectively due to three fundamental bottlenecks: performance degradation, system overhead, and limited generalizability. First, from performance perspective, compressing full-context attention into bounded or fixed-size states inevitably induces information decay and fails to retain fine-grained details over long horizons. Second, from cost perspective, long-term memory methods such as M+ (Wang et al., 2025a) overlook cache compression, as maintaining multi-layer KV caches and repeatedly fetching states across layers incur heavy storage overhead and communication latency. Third, from generalizability perspective, prior memory architectures are typically tailored either to pretraining from scratch (Behrouz et al., 2025) or to post-training adaptation, lacking versatility across both paradigms. To tackle these challenges, MemOnce couples compact final-layer memory encoding with efficient memory retrieval and on-demand KV decoding, and is validated across both pretraining and post-training adaptation. Our experimental results demonstrate that learning scalable, reusable memory states provides viable path toward next-generation foundation architectures.

sections.title: 5.2 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Several limitations of MemOnce offer valuable directions for future research. First, constrained by available computing resources, our pre-training from scratch is conducted up to the 1B parameter scale; validating the foundational scaling behavior of MemOnce via full pre-training at larger scales (e.g., 7B or beyond) remains future work. Second, while MemOnce demonstrates strong memory capabilities, its performance in downstream agent tasks remains to be fully validated, particularly in complex scenarios such as long-horizon interactive coding and multi-step tool use. In future work, we plan to pre-train MemOnce at larger parameter scales and explore its potential across broader continual interactive scenarios.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we present MemOnce, foundational memory architecture that achieves accurate long-context recall, linear-time complexity, and constant active memory states for continual language modeling. By coupling the memory encoder-decoder and memory sparse attention designs, MemOnce caches and retrieves memory states only once while dynamically decoding them into multi-layer KV caches on demand. MemOnce seamlessly integrates into pretrained models to accelerate inference while establishing itself as the first native memory model to surpass full-context baselines. Extensive experiments across diverse training paradigms, model scales, and context lengths demonstrate its effectiveness and generality.

A Related Work
sections.content: A.1 Architectural and Attention Optimizations To alleviate the quadratic compute and linear KV cache growth of standard Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), architectural reforms have progressed along three lines. First, from linear to hybrid architectures: linear and recurrent models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023), RWKV (Peng et al., 2023), and Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025) compress history into fixed-size states for constant-memory, linear-time inference, but struggle with fine-grained in-context recall (Jelassi et al., 2024). To balance computational efficiency with accurate recall of historical information, modern backbones increasingly adopt hybrid designs: Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) and Kimi K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026) interleave linear or gated delta layers with periodic global attention, while MiMo (Xiaomi, 2026) interleaves sliding-window attention with full attention. Second, from intra-layer sparse mechanisms, such as Native Sparse Attention (NSA) (Yuan global to sparse attention: 1 et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026a) and block-sparse routing (Qiu et al., 2026), dynamically prune attention matrices via hardware-aligned compressed, selected, and sliding-window branches. Third, cross-layer KV cache reuse: architectures like YOCO (Sun et al., 2024b) and HySparse (Gao et al., 2026) cache KV states at an intermediate anchor layer and feed them forward to subsequent layers, whereas LastKV (Cai et al., 2026) directly reuses raw final-layer KV states across earlier layers. Despite these gains, hybrid and sparse models still retain multi-layer KV caches, with sparse mechanisms further incurring repeated routing overhead across layers and decoding steps, while cross-layer sharing methods still retain full-length token states without sequence compression. A.2 Native Memory Models Native memory models internalize historical context into compact parametric or latent states. One category compresses history into fixed-capacity representations: Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025) updates deep neural memory at test time via surprise-driven gradients with momentum and weight decay; δ-Mem (Lei et al., 2026) updates low-dimensional state matrices online via delta-rule learning; Metis (Zhang et al., 2026) embeds persistent, gradient-free memory states directly into the backbone in single forward pass; and EvoEmbedding (Nie et al., 2026a) maintains window-based latent memory queue for long-context representation learning. To overcome fixed capacity limits, second category dynamically expands the state pool: M+ (Wang et al., 2025a) extends MemoryLLM (Wang et al., 2024) with long-term latent pool and layer-wise co-trained retrievers; and Memory Caching (Behrouz et al., 2026) caches recurrent states at segment boundaries for gated residual aggregation. Nevertheless, these methods either suffer from fixed-capacity bottlenecks or incur retrieval overhead, and their prevalent reliance on post-training adaptation often induces catastrophic forgetting. A.3 External Memory Systems External memory systems decouple persistent memory storage and management from the model backbone, representing historical experiences in explicit stores and handling memory construction, updating, and retrieval through dedicated pipelines (Hu et al., 2025). Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) dynamically extracts and consolidates salient conversational facts for subsequent retrieval, while A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026b) employs agent-driven note construction and dynamic linking to organize memories into an evolving knowledge network. For multimodal personalization, PersonaVLM (Nie et al., 2026b) integrates proactive multimodal memory accumulation and multi-turn memory-grounded reasoning with dynamic personality profiling for response alignment. To improve memory construction efficiency, LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) introduces lightweight sensory-level compression, topic-aware segmentation and summarization, and offline sleep-time consolidation. For streaming video understanding, Light-Omni (Nie et al., 2026c) employs dual-state architecture, combining non-parametric global state distilled from episodic memory with parametric latent state that enables reflexive action control and semantically aligned retrieval without iterative reasoning. Despite these advances, long-term memories are still largely maintained in external stores or auxiliary memory structures, with memory construction, consolidation, and retrieval handled through separate procedures. This separation can introduce additional storage and orchestration overhead while making it less straightforward to jointly optimize memory formation, maintenance, and utilization with the backbone, particularly under end-to-end objectives such as reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2025b). A.4 Comparison with Existing Methods MemOnce addresses the limitations across all three paradigms. Compared with architectural and cross-layer KV optimizations, MemOnce caches only small subset of final-layer hidden states and performs sparse retrieval only once per query, eliminating both layer-wise storage and routing overhead. Compared with native and external memory systems, MemOnce enables efficient end-to-end optimization and long-term memory capabilities for both pretraining and post-training adaptation. Furthermore, decoding compact memory states into KV caches effectively preserves long-range context without catastrophic forgetting.

sections.content: C.1 MemOnce-1M To jointly optimize MemOnces memory encoder-decoder and single-shot sparse retrieval, we construct largescale multi-turn training corpus, MemOnce-1M (1M samples). Every training instance is standardized into multi-turn conversational sequence = {x1, x2, . . . , xt1, xt}, consisting of = 1 historical interaction rounds followed by target query turn xt. To obtain high-fidelity supervision for both language modeling and memory retrieval without costly manual annotation, we employ Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as teacher model for the final user query xt. Conditioned on the complete dialogue history, the teacher model simultaneously generates: (i) grounded reference response yt to supervise the language modeling objective, and (ii) the exact indices of historical evidence turns + {1, . . . , h} containing the supporting facts required to answer the query. These distilled evidence annotations directly supervise the contrastive retrieval loss in Eq. (11), aligning the query descriptor ϕ(hL ) with relevant historical index vectors {ϕ(hL )}h i=1 . C.2 Data Composition As illustrated in Figure 5(c), our training corpus integrates eight complementary data sources to balance long-range factual recall, multi-hop reasoning, and conversational fluency: Long-Context Representation and Memory Corpora (64.2%): The largest portion of the dataset is derived from EvoTrain-180K (Nie et al., 2026a) (38.5%) and LiveMem3 (25.7%), which provide rich multi-session dialogues and dense long-range retrieval supervision across diverse domains. 3https://huggingface.co/datasets/chen-l/LiveMem-SFT 4 (a) Distribution of history rounds (h). (b) Distribution of sequence lengths. (c) Data source composition. Figure 5 Statistics of MemOnce-1M. (a) Percentage of samples across historical dialogue rounds [3, 464]. (b) Token sequence length distribution with mean of 7, 099 tokens and 90th percentile (p90) of 16, 426 tokens. (c) Proportion of the eight constituent data sources. Multi-Hop and Long-Context Instruction Datasets (25.0%): To strengthen complex reasoning over retrieved memory states, we incorporate ChatQA-24 (11.0%), LongMIT-SFT5 (6.0%), 2WikiMultiHopQA6 (5.0%), Step-3.5-Flash-SFT7 (2.8%), and δ-Mem Qasper (Lei et al., 2026)8 (0.2%). Raw long-document QA pairs are segmented into sequential conversational turns so that supporting paragraphs are distributed across separate historical segments. Synthetic Data (10.8%): Following the data synthesis methodology of EvoEmbedding (Nie et al., 2026a), we construct an additional 10.8% of synthetic multi-turn samples (Synthetic (Ours)) via structured template-based question generation. Specifically, we plant multi-source factual chains, evolving user states, and entity attributes across distant dialogue turns using controllable templates, and interleave semantically similar hard-negative distractor turns in between. Positional shortcuts (e.g., explicit turn-index references) are systematically stripped during synthesis, forcing the indexing module and backbone to rely strictly on semantic matching and cross-segment reasoning. C.3 Statistical Analysis Figures 5(a) and 5(b) present the structural statistics of the dataset across historical conversation rounds and token lengths: Historical Rounds (h): As shown in Figure 5(a), the number of historical rounds spans from 3 to 464 turns. While short-to-medium dialogues (310 and 1120 rounds) account for 12.4% and 24.0% of the corpus (activating full-window supervision fallback to stabilize early ϕ() training), over 63% of the samples exceed MemOnces 16-segment short-term sliding window Gshort . Specifically, medium-horizon dialogues (2160 rounds) constitute 25.8%, long-horizon sessions (61200 rounds) account for 25.4%, and ultra-long multi-session histories (201464 rounds) make up the remaining 12.4%. This heavy-tailed distribution ensures that the model is rigorously trained to retrieve evicted memory representations from the long-term pool Glong . Context Lengths: Figure 5(b) depicts the token length distribution across dialogue trajectories, exhibiting multi-modal long-tail profile up to 25, 000 tokens, with mean of 7,099 tokens, 90th-percentile (p90) of 16,426 tokens, and high-density clusters around 10K12K and 16K tokens. sections.title: D Experimental Details
sections.content: D.1 Training and Implementation Details Pre-training Details. To evaluate architectural design choices from scratch, we pre-train our base models on FineWeb-Edu-10B (Lozhkov et al., 2024) for one full epoch, tokenized with the Llama-2 BPE tokenizer (Touvron et al., 2023) (vocabulary size 32,000). All models are optimized with fused AdamW under 2,000-step linear warmup followed by cosine decay, on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The full configurations are summarized in Table 7. Post-training and Memory Adaptation. For the main models across the Qwen3.5 hybrid family (2B and 4B), we freeze the pretrained backbone and perform memory-aware post-training on MemOnce-1M for one epoch on an 8 NVIDIA H100 node with Distributed Data Parallel and activation checkpointing, following the configurations in Table 7. For representation and reranking evaluations, our testing protocol strictly follows EvoEmbedding (Nie et al., 2026a). Trainable Modules and Optimization Settings. Across the Qwen3.5 hybrid backbones (2B and 4B), post-training adaptation introduces three lightweight trainable components while keeping the base model frozen: 1. Memory LoRA Adapter: Low-rank adapters (r = 128, α = 256, dropout 0.05) attached to the attention projections, activated exclusively during memory encoding (gθ) and query descriptor extraction, and disabled during response generation. 2. Indexing Projection ϕ(): two-layer SiLU MLP mapping the terminal token state of each segment from hidden dimension to de = 1024 for cosine similarity routing (τ = 0.1, retrieval budget = 64). 3. On-Demand Decoders (uθ): For full-attention layers only (e.g., 8 of 32 layers in Qwen3.5-4B), trainable projections, and key normalization, initialized from the ] into layer-specific KV caches Ct. The model is optimized end-to-end under Eq. (11) with λ = 0.1 and τ = 0.1 (computing the contrastive loss over all available historical states when the dialogue fits entirely within Gshort copies of the input LayerNorm, frozen backbone, decode the active memory state Mt = [M long Gshort Proj/V Proj ). D.2 Memory Benchmarks We evaluate MemOnce across six complementary benchmarks spanning short-context state updates to million-token multi-session interactions: MemBench9 (Tan et al., 2025): To assess precise state tracking and fact overwriting without long-context dilution, we adopt the Knowledge Update (KU) subset of MemBench, which comprises 2, 000 evaluation 9https://github.com/import-myself/Membench 6 instances with an average history length of approximately 4K tokens. LoCoMo10 (Maharana et al., 2024): multi-session conversational memory benchmark consisting of 10 extended daily-life dialogues, each spanning roughly 30 sessions. The model assumes the role of one speaker and must concisely answer questions regarding specific biographical and event details of both participants based on the entire conversation history. Following standard evaluation practice, we filter out the unanswerable adversarial category (Category 5), resulting in 1, 540 evaluation questions. LongMemEval11 (Wu et al., 2025): comprehensive multi-session memory benchmark covering five core memory capabilities (single-session recall, multi-session synthesis, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention), containing 500 questions each paired with approximately 115K tokens of timestamped multi-session history. PersonaMem-128 (Jiang et al., 2025): long-context memory benchmark sharing the same data distribution and four-way multiple-choice task formulation as PersonaMem-1M, designed to evaluate fine-grained recall of user-disclosed facts and preferences over 1, 000 test questions within 128K-token context horizon. PersonaMem-1M12 (Jiang et al., 2025): An ultra-long-range personalized memory stress test comprising 500 four-way multiple-choice questions. Each instance requires tracking implicit user facts, evolving preferences, and persona details across 32 conversational sessions totaling approximately 1M tokens. HotpotQA-1M: multi-hop QA benchmark constructed from HotpotQA13 (Yang et al., 2018) to evaluate long-context memory capabilities. It is synthesized by aggregating 9, 848 raw validation passages (approximately 1.35M tokens) while retaining 500 open-ended multi-hop questions whose supporting evidence resides completely within the aggregated memory bank. D.3 Evaluation Protocol For multiple-choice benchmarks (MemBench, PersonaMem-128, and PersonaMem-1M), we report exact accuracy. For open-ended QA and conversational benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and HotpotQA-1M), we follow the official LLM-as-a-Judge protocols specified by each benchmark to ensure fair comparison. Specifically, we adopt benchmark-native binary grading prompts (e.g., tailored prompt (Nie et al., 2026a) templates for LongMemEval and LoCoMo) to evaluate whether the generated response entails the groundtruth answer. Empirical verification confirms that employing these official benchmark-aligned prompts yields consistent relative performance trends without affecting the core conclusions. The standard binary evaluation prompt is shown below: will give you question, correct answer, and response from model. Please answer yes if the response contains the correct answer. Otherwise, answer no. If the response is equivalent to the correct answer or contains all the intermediate steps to get the correct answer, you should also answer yes. If the response only contains subset of the information required by the answer, answer no. Question: {question} Correct Answer: {answer} Model Response: {response} Is the model response correct? sections.title: E Ablation Study
sections.content: E.1 Compression Ratio We first evaluate the trade-off between the compression ratio {1, 2, 4, 8} and downstream accuracy in Table 8. Increasing from 1 to 8 compresses the persistent memory bank Gt by 8 along the sequence dimension, while causing only negligible accuracy drop of 0.0025 (0.5280 0.5255 when linear states are persisted) and 0.0028 (0.5263 0.5235 when discarded). This confirms that the trailing 1/r final-layer hidden states effectively encapsulate segment-level semantics, allowing = 8 to serve as our default setting. E.2 Linear State Persistence Table 8 also examines whether the recurrent states of linear layers need to be maintained across historical segments. The Persisted setting carries linear recurrent states across segments alongside Gt, whereas the Discarded setting resets linear states at segment boundaries and relies solely on the decoded KV caches from Mt for long-range context. Across all compression ratios, both settings yield nearly identical performance (e.g., 0.5255 vs. 0.5235 at = 8), demonstrating that long-range information is predominantly preserved by our expandable memory bank Gt rather than fixed-capacity linear states. We therefore discard cross-segment linear states by default, which eliminates multi-layer recurrent state storage. E.3 Top-K Retrieval Budget We next analyze the sensitivity of MemOnce to the retrieval budget {0, 16, 32, 64, 128} across five long-context memory benchmarks  (Table 9)  . At = 0, the model relies solely on the short-term window without long-term retrieval, resulting in low average score of 36.83. Retrieving just = 16 long-term Gshort representations yields substantial gain of +22.89 points (59.72), verifying the high information density of our compact memory states. Performance peaks at = 64 (60.07), capturing sufficient multi-session evidence for multi-hop and temporal queries in LoCoMo (67.01) and LongMemEval (47.40). Further expanding to 128 slightly reduces the average score to 58.86 while doubling the retrieval footprint, as excessive low-relevance states introduce contextual noise. Consequently, we adopt = 64 as the default retrieval budget. 8 Figure 6 Pre-training dynamics across the four parameter tiers.
